---
title: "Engineering log"
---

Design decisions, refactors, numerical stability issues, data layout and
performance choices. It supplements the git history with the reasoning.
Entries are dated H2 sections; existing entries are never edited.

## 2026-11-05: Step 0, project scaffolding

**Double precision.** `jax_enable_x64` is set in `jaxdft/_config.py`, the
first import in `jaxdft/__init__.py`. Any entry point that imports anything
from the package therefore enables x64 before any array exists. The test suite
checks this in a fresh subprocess as well as in-process, because
`tests/conftest.py` imports `jaxdft` for every test and would otherwise hide a
broken import order.

`jaxdft.precision.assert_double_precision` walks a pytree and rejects any
inexact leaf that is not float64 or complex128. Integer and boolean leaves
(Miller indices, masks) are ignored. Physics tests should call it on their
outputs. This is how "a test must fail if any physical array is float32" is
enforced in practice.

**Test configuration.**

- `--import-mode=importlib`, so the three test directories can contain
  files with the same name without `__init__.py` packages.
- `filterwarnings = error`: a warning from JAX (e.g. an implicit dtype
  truncation) fails the test rather than scrolling past.
- `--strict-markers`, with one marker, `slow`, defined up front.
- Hypothesis runs with `deadline=None`, because the first call of a jitted
  function includes tracing and compilation, so per-example timing is
  meaningless. Two profiles: `default` (50 examples, for laptops) and `ci`
  (200), selected with `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE`.

**Dependencies.** `pytest` and `hypothesis` are in the `dev` group, `altair`
and `jupyter` in `docs`. Both are uv default groups, since the definition of
done needs both, so a plain `uv sync` installs everything.

**Docs execution.** `execute.freeze` is explicitly `false`. Documents compute
their numbers from `jaxdft` at render time, and freezing would let a document
go stale against the code without failing.

Quarto must find the project's virtual environment. It does when the venv is
active (it then picks `.venv/bin/python3` from `PATH`). From a plain shell it
falls back to the system Python and fails. I tried a `docs/_environment` file
setting `QUARTO_PYTHON`. Quarto resolves that relative path against the
directory it is invoked from, not the project, so it broke depending on where
the command was run, and I removed it. `uv run quarto render docs/` works from
any shell and is the robust form of the definition-of-done command.

**Removed.** The `jaxdft` console-script entry point and its `main()`
placeholder from the `uv init` template. A command-line interface will be
added when there is something to run.

**Deferred.**

- The shared plot-style module arrives with the first plot (Milestone 1a
  validation). It will live outside the physics so that `altair` stays a docs
  dependency.
- A `units` module with tested conversions arrives with the first
  boundary conversion. Milestone 1a works entirely in atomic units and in
  units of $\tfrac12(2\pi/a)^2$.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1a design decisions from theory review

The [theory post](../theory/01a_empty_lattice.qmd) was reviewed before any
implementation. Every quantitative claim was re-derived independently, and no
physics errors were found. The review changed four engineering decisions.
I reproduced its measurements with a throwaway NumPy enumeration before
accepting them.

**Per-k padded Miller-index lists, not a shared candidate set.** `vmap` needs
a common shape, not a common set of G vectors. The first draft proposed one
set containing every $\mathcal{B}_\mathbf{k}$ (radius $G_\text{max} + |\mathrm{W}|$)
plus a per-k mask. For fcc with $a = 10.26$ Bohr over the six high-symmetry
points, that set was 1.73× the largest per-k basis at 5 Ha and 1.17× at 80 Ha.
Dense `eigh` costs the cube of that: 5.1× and 1.6×. The per-k sizes
themselves differ by about 2%. The batch layout is therefore
`(n_k, N_pad, 3)` integer Miller indices plus an `(n_k, N_pad)` boolean mask.
`N_pad` is a Python int fixed on the host before tracing. These numbers are a
one-off snapshot for the decision record; the validation document computes
them from the library.

**Padding is exactly decoupled, and the sentinel is modest.** Padded components
must have zero rows and columns, not just a large diagonal. Otherwise
$\tilde V(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}')$ in 1b, evaluated at a padding entry's
arbitrary Miller index, would leak into the physical block. The sentinel
diagonal is a small multiple of $E_\text{cut}$. The reviewer measured that LAPACK's
physical eigenvalues are insensitive to the sentinel (1.9e-13 Ha for sentinels
from 4e1 to 1e12). A huge sentinel would still spread the spectrum over many
orders of magnitude, which slows down the iterative solvers planned later.
The test is solver-independent: the same k-point with two values of `N_pad`
must give the same bands.

**Provable enumeration bound.** The integer search box is
$|m_i| \le \lceil (G_\text{max}+|\mathbf{k}|)|\mathbf{a}_i|/2\pi \rceil$, from
$\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{a}_i = 2\pi m_i$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. A guessed cube is
unsafe in skewed cells.

**Cutoff ties.** Test cutoffs are placed strictly between shells, with a
relative margin of at least 1e-8. The reviewer suggested instead making the
reference enumeration use the code's own arithmetic, so ties round the same
way. I did not adopt that, because it makes the reference less independent of
the code it checks.

**Basis-size bound.** The reviewer flagged that a test asserting monotone
convergence of $N_\text{PW}$ to its asymptote would be flaky, and proposed a
bound $C\,E_\text{cut}^{-1/2}$ with $C$ measured once. I used a rigorous bound
instead, from tiling with Brillouin zones of circumradius $r_\text{BZ}$, which
needs no fitted constant. A first version used the reciprocal parallelepiped's
diameter (2.03 Bohr⁻¹ at $a = 10.26$). It held, but was nearly vacuous: the
upper bound was 4.4 at 5 Ha. The Wigner–Seitz circumradius $|\mathrm{W}|$
(0.68 Bohr⁻¹) is three times tighter. It is still loose and catches only
gross errors; the exact count is tested by enumeration.

**References.** Cutoff conventions as documented for DFTK (`Ecut`), ABINIT
(`ecut`) and Quantum ESPRESSO (`ecutwfc`, `ecutrho`). No source code was
consulted.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1a public API, agreed before implementation

The acceptance tests fix the public API, so it was settled in a question round
with the project lead before any code was written. Each decision below names
the option that was chosen.

**Layout.** Subpackages by role in the calculation, not a flat set of modules.
The main names are re-exported from `jaxdft`.

```
jaxdft/
  structure/    lattice.py (Lattice)   kpoints.py (special_points_fcc, kpath, KPath)
  basis/        planewave.py (PlaneWaveBasis)
  hamiltonian/  operator.py (Hamiltonian, hamiltonian, apply_H, dense_matrix)
                kinetic.py (Kinetic)
  solvers/      eigen.py (dense_eigensolver)
  calculations/ bands.py (band_structure, Bands)
  analytic/     free_electron.py (free_electron_bands)
```

XC, pseudopotentials and IO will get their own subpackages, so that the SCF
loop never imports them by name.

**Data.**

- `Lattice` is a frozen dataclass registered as a pytree. Its only leaf is
  `vectors` (rows, Bohr); `reciprocal` and `volume` are derived. `grad` of a
  function of a `Lattice` returns a `Lattice`, which keeps cell derivatives
  possible later. Input is converted to float64.
- k-points are **fractional** (k = f·B) at every public interface.
- `PlaneWaveBasis` stores only integers and masks: `miller` with shape
  (n_k, N_pad, 3), `mask` with shape (n_k, N_pad), fractional `kpoints`, and
  the static `ecut` and `n_pad`. Cartesian k+G and kinetic energies are
  computed from a `Lattice` when needed, so the path from the cell to the
  energies stays differentiable. The basis is purely combinatorial.
- One batched basis holds all k-points. `basis[i]` returns the same class with
  the k axis removed, which is also what `vmap` hands the mapped function.
- `N_pad` defaults to exactly max_k N_PW and can be overridden with `n_pad=`.
  If it is smaller than that, construction raises `ValueError`. Bucketing
  waits until profiling shows recompilation matters.

**Operators and solver.**

- A Hamiltonian term is a pytree with `prepare(lattice, basis_k)`, which
  returns a prepared pytree with `apply(psi)`. `hamiltonian()` prepares every
  term once per k, so iterative solvers do not repeat the setup on every
  apply. Terms never see padding.
- `apply_H(ham, psi)` acts on blocks `psi` of shape (N_pad, n). It masks the
  input, sums the terms, masks the output, and adds `s·psi` on padded entries.
  Decoupling is therefore enforced centrally, so a new term cannot leak by
  forgetting a mask. The tests require ecut < s ≤ 10·ecut.
- `dense_eigensolver(apply, dim, n_bands)` takes any linear operator and knows
  nothing about plane waves.
- `band_structure(lattice, basis, n_bands, terms=(Kinetic(),), solver=dense_eigensolver)`
  returns `Bands(eigenvalues, eigenvectors, kpoints, basis)`. Eigenvalues have
  shape (n_k, n_bands) in Hartree; eigenvectors have shape
  (n_k, N_pad, n_bands) and are zero on padding. The function raises
  `ValueError` if n_bands > min_k N_PW.

**k-paths.** `special_points_fcc()` returns a dict from label to fractional k,
with ASCII keys (`"G"` for Γ). `kpath(lattice, points, segments, n_points)`
spreads exactly `n_points` points over the segments by Cartesian length. It
returns `KPath(kpoints, distance, tick_positions, tick_labels)`. The tick
labels use Γ, and a break is labelled `"U|K"`; the distance does not advance
across a break.

**Analytic reference.** `jaxdft.analytic.free_electron_bands` exists so that
the validation document can use it without reimplementing physics. The tests
never trust it. They compare it with `tests/support/free_electron.py`, an
independent NumPy enumeration over twice the proven Miller bound, which is
itself checked against the hand-derived degeneracy table.

**Spec gap found while writing the tests.** With a non-diagonal term, physical
eigenvalues can exceed ecut, and the sentinel is only guaranteed to be above
ecut. So the requested bands are guaranteed physical only below ecut. This is
exactly the theory post's rule ("tests compare only eigenvalues below the
cutoff"). The tests follow it everywhere, and the test-only coupling term is
kept weak (a Gershgorin bound of about 0.16 Ha). Requesting all N_PW bands with
a strong potential is legitimate input, but it may return sentinel
eigenvalues.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1a implementation

**Pytrees.** `Lattice` and `PlaneWaveBasis` are pytree classes whose
`tree_unflatten` bypasses `__init__`. JAX rebuilds pytrees with tracers,
cotangents and placeholder objects, and validation or dtype conversion in
`__init__` would break on those. Input conversion (to float64, shape checks)
therefore happens only on user construction. `ecut` and `n_pad` are static aux
data of the basis, so changing the cutoff retraces. That is intended, since
the shapes change with it anyway. Prepared terms and `Hamiltonian` use
`register_dataclass`; the sentinel is a static field.

**Basis construction without a k loop.** `PlaneWaveBasis.build` enumerates one
integer box from the proven bound, using the largest |k| in the batch. It
evaluates ½|(f+m)B|² for every k at once, then compacts each row with a stable
`argsort` of the inverted mask. Real entries come first and padding takes
Miller index 0. This runs eagerly on the host, because the output shape depends
on the data. The box is shared across k, which wastes some work when the
k-points differ a lot in |k|. That matters only for construction, not for the
padded arrays the physics sees.

**Operator and solver.**

- `apply_H` is the only place that knows about padding (the sentinel is
  2·ecut).
- `dense_eigensolver` symmetrises the matrix it builds before `eigh`. This
  costs nothing and removes rounding-level anti-Hermitian parts that a future
  term could introduce.
- `band_structure` zeroes eigenvectors on padding explicitly. With LAPACK
  `eigh` on an exactly decoupled block this is already true bit for bit (a
  mutation test confirmed it). The explicit mask makes it a guarantee for
  solvers that don't share that property.
- The whole band structure is one `jit` over a `vmap` over k, with `n_bands`
  and the solver static.

**Mutation testing of the acceptance suite.** The tests had never been run
against an implementation, so a clean first pass proved little. I planted bugs
one at a time and checked that the suite caught them. Each of these was caught:

- terms seeing padded input
- coupled padding rows
- a sentinel far above 10·ecut
- an enumeration bound that ignores |k|
- a 1e-7 error in the kinetic prefactor
- a missing transpose in B
- a 2% cutoff error

Two changes were not caught, both by design:

- `<=` versus `<` in the cutoff test, since tests never put a cutoff on a
  shell.
- A cutoff error of 0.1%. Test cutoffs sit mid-gap, so it selects the same
  plane waves and is physically unobservable.

**Validation document.**

- In the empty lattice, the computed eigenvalues agree bit for bit with the
  library's analytic reference. `eigh` on a diagonal matrix returns the
  diagonal, and both evaluate the same expression. The document says so rather
  than presenting it as a tolerance check.
- The document asserts its own interpretive claims (degeneracies match,
  deviation within tolerance), so a regression breaks the render rather than
  leaving stale prose.

**Plotting and dependencies.** The shared style lives in `jaxdft.plotting.style`.
Inside the package, the docs can import it without `sys.path` manipulation.
It imports altair lazily, and nothing in the physics imports it. It disables
altair's 5000-row cap, because band structures are a few thousand points.
`pandas` joins the `docs` group. I checked the charts visually by rendering
their Vega-Lite specs to PNG with `vl-convert`, in a throwaway environment.
That is not a project dependency.

## 2026-11-05: Test correction, kinetic diagonal tolerance at k+G = 0

Hypothesis found a case where the property test
`test_empty_lattice_physical_block_is_kinetic_diagonal` failed: a cubic cell
with k = (1,1,1) fractional, so one plane wave has k+G = 0 exactly. The two
arithmetic routes, $(\mathbf{f}+\mathbf{m})B$ in the package and
$\mathbf{k} + \mathbf{m}B$ in the test, both round to a kinetic energy of order
1e-32 Ha. The test's purely relative tolerance (`rtol=1e-13`, `atol=0`) cannot
accept rounding at an exact zero. This was a defect in the test, not the code.
I raised it before changing anything, and the agreed fix adds `atol = 1e-14·ecut`,
which follows the theory post's argument that rounding scales with
$\|H_\text{phys}\| \le E_\text{cut}$. The falsifying case is pinned as an
explicit `@example`. I audited the other relative-only comparisons: they either
compare exact zeros with exact zeros or involve no zeros.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1b design decisions from theory review

The [1b theory post](../theory/01b_cohen_bergstresser.qmd) was reviewed before
implementation, and the review is kept in `docs/theory/reviews/`. It confirmed
the normalisation. I checked its sharpest claims independently, with a
throwaway NumPy model, before acting on them.

**Matrix-free local potential.** The first draft proposed storing a dense
$\tilde V(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}')$ per k-point. That is $O(N^2)$ per k, multiplied
by $n_k$ under `vmap`, and it is a stored matrix rather than an operator. Each
row has at most 44 non-zeros (shells 3, 8 and 11), independently of the
cutoff. So `prepare` builds a per-k neighbour table and `apply` is a gather and
a sum. The neighbour search runs inside `jit`/`vmap` and so must be jittable:
sorted integer Miller keys plus `searchsorted`, not a host dictionary. Dense
matrices are built only from the operator, as in 1a.

**Off-shell guard in physical units.** The guard must compare $|\mathbf{G}|^2$
in Bohr⁻² against the shells at $a_\text{CB}$. Dimensionless shell indices are
invariant under isotropic scaling, so a guard on them would accept any lattice
constant. The review pointed this out; my draft had the reason subtly wrong.

**Kept: physical-unit shell matching, not integer cubic indices.** The review
proposed exact integer keys. They are exact for fcc only, and the separation
between shells makes a $10^{-8}$ relative window unambiguous anyway.

**Tests sharpened.**

- The indirect gap is tested as the minimum along Δ, with an interiority
  check. The level at X lies within the tolerance of the paper's value, so a
  test of the level at X would pass on the wrong quantity.
- Inversion parity gives the first eigenvector test, as a trace over the
  level's projector.
- Pairing is tested along the X–W line, with a negative control at a generic
  face point.
- The test cutoff is 6 Ha, where all Table I splittings have converged to
  about 1 meV.
- Physics tolerances are 0.15 or 0.25 eV per entry, derived from the paper's
  stated rounding and convergence. Numerical tolerances are 1e-10 Ha for
  eigenvalue comparisons and 1e-8 Ha for grouping degenerate levels.

**Not adopted.** A test of the minimum's position (0.855 X ± 0.01) would be a
regression value: the only sources are our own model and a secondary
reproduction of the same model. It is reported in the validation document
instead. DFTK is deferred to the SCF milestone.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1b public API, agreed before implementation

Settled in four question rounds with the project lead before any 1b test or
code was written. The changes to the 1a API were approved as part of these
rounds.

**The system object is `Structure`, not `Lattice`.** `Structure` is a pytree:
a `Lattice`, fractional `positions` with shape (n_atoms, 3) as a leaf, per-atom
`weights` with shape (n_atoms,) as a leaf defaulting to 1, and static `species`
labels. It represents any periodic configuration: a bulk crystal, a slab, or a
molecule in a vacuum box. "Crystal" was rejected because it reads oddly for the
last two. Positions are always stored fractional. The decisions that follow:

- `Structure.from_cartesian(cell, positions, species, unit=...)` takes the cell
  and positions in the same unit, `"Angstrom"` or `"Bohr"`. There is no default,
  so every call states its unit. It converts once.
- Weights are not range-checked. Their physical range is [0, 1], but
  finite-difference checks at λ = 1 need to step past it.
- Atoms are mapped to pseudopotentials by species label, through a dict held by
  the term.
- Factories live in a subpackage, one module each:
  `structure/builders/{fcc,diamond,empty}.py`. `Lattice.fcc` moves there as
  `fcc_lattice`, so `Lattice` keeps only its general constructor. Code used by
  several builders goes in a shared module when it appears.
- The term protocol becomes `prepare(structure, basis_k)`, and
  `band_structure(structure, basis, ...)` and `hamiltonian(structure, ...)`
  follow. The 1a tests are updated mechanically. The empty lattice is
  `empty(lattice)`. `PlaneWaveBasis.build`, `kpath` and `free_electron_bands`
  keep taking a `Lattice`, because they involve no atoms.

**Pseudopotential protocol** (and the matching update to `CLAUDE.md`). The
literal `(G) -> (V_loc, V_nl)` signature was dropped after a discussion. The
two parts are different kinds of object: a local form factor v̂(q), against
nonlocal projectors depending on k+G and k+G′ separately. A tuple would force
us to guess the nonlocal interface before anything exists to test it. The
protocol is now:

- `local(q) -> v̂(q)`: the atomic Fourier transform, in Ha·Bohr³,
  cell-independent. The `LocalPotential` term applies
  Ṽ(G) = Ω⁻¹ Σⱼ λⱼ e^{−iG·τⱼ} v̂ⱼ(|G|).
- `local_support: float | None`: the q beyond which v̂ is exactly zero.
  `None` means unbounded. The gather-based term refuses an unbounded
  pseudopotential, pointing to the FFT term that comes with SCF.
- An optional host-side `validate(...)` hook. `band_structure` calls
  `term.validate(structure)` before tracing, and `LocalPotential` forwards it
  to each pseudopotential. Cohen–Bergstresser raises if a non-zero |G|² within
  its support is off its tabulated shells, comparing in physical units.
- Nonlocal methods are added, additively, in the milestone that first needs
  them, with their own Hamiltonian term.

**Cohen–Bergstresser.** `jaxdft.pseudo.cohen_bergstresser.silicon()` returns
a `CohenBergstresser` holding a_CB and the form factors in publication units
(Å, Ry), converted at construction. Only Si is included, so no untested data
ships.

**Units.** `jaxdft/units.py` holds CODATA 2022 constants and a `convert`
helper. Units are cross-cutting (structure, pseudo, plotting), so no
subpackage owns them.

**Analysis.** A `jaxdft/analysis/` subpackage holds the tools both tests and
docs need: degenerate-level grouping, inversion parity, the VBM energy
reference, and the minimum of a band along a segment. The minimum is found by
dense vmapped sampling followed by bracketed golden-section refinement on the
host. An autodiff-based search (via group velocities) was deferred to a
dedicated milestone: the k-dependent basis makes dE/dk well defined only
within a fixed basis.

**Reference data.** `reference/cohen_bergstresser_1966/si_table1.json` holds
Table I's Si row, in eV as printed, with experiment and calculation separate,
a tolerance class per entry, and source metadata. A README says it was
transcribed by hand from the scan.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1b acceptance tests and the signature details they fix

The tests follow the API agreed in the question rounds. Writing them fixed the
following details, listed here so none slips in unannounced.

- **Top-level re-exports** add `Structure`, `LocalPotential`, `diamond`,
  `empty` and `fcc_lattice`. Pseudopotentials, `units` and `analysis` are
  imported from their modules.
- **`Structure`.**
  - Signature: `Structure(lattice, positions, species, weights=None)`, with
    `.n_atoms`, `.cartesian_positions` (derived) and `species` as a tuple.
  - `from_cartesian(cell, positions, species, unit, weights=None)`, where an
    unknown unit raises `ValueError`.
  - `empty(lattice).lattice is lattice`.
- **Builders.** `fcc_lattice(a, unit)` and `diamond(a, species, unit)`.
  The unit is a required argument.
- **Units.** `BOHR_IN_ANGSTROM`, `HARTREE_IN_EV`, `RYDBERG_IN_HARTREE`, and
  `convert(value, from_unit, to_unit)`. Unit names are case-sensitive:
  `"Bohr"`, `"Angstrom"`, `"Hartree"`, `"Rydberg"`, `"eV"`. Mixed dimensions
  raise.
- **Cohen–Bergstresser.**
  - `silicon()` exposes `lattice_constant_angstrom`, `form_factors_ry`
    (keys 3, 8, 11), `lattice_constant` (Bohr) and `shell_q`, the physical
    shell radii in Bohr⁻¹.
  - `local(q)` returns the tabulated v̂ on shells 3, 8 and 11. Everywhere
    else it returns 0, so traced code and autodiff through `jnp.where` stay
    NaN-free.
  - `validate(q_values)` raises on any q within the support that is off the
    table.
  - **Shell 4 counts as off-table.** CB never fitted it. It drops out of
    perfect diamond only because S = 0 there. So unequal weights, or a single
    atom, which make S ≠ 0 at shell 4, are refused.
- **`LocalPotential`.**
  - `coefficients(structure, miller)` returns Ṽ(mB) in complex128. It is
    public, used for the real-space phase-sign check and the docs.
  - `validate(structure)` raises `ValueError` for a species without a
    pseudopotential and `NotImplementedError` for unbounded support. It
    forwards to the pseudopotential only the q at which that species'
    structure factor is non-zero. So a perfect 8-atom conventional cell is
    accepted, and the same cell with one weight changed is refused.
  - Matrix-free bound: the prepared term holds at most 256·N_pad elements.
- **Analysis.**
  - `group_levels(eigenvalues, atol)` returns `[(level, degeneracy)]`.
  - `inversion_parities(bands, k_index, atol=1e-8)` returns
    `[(level, degeneracy, parity)]`. It raises unless 2k is a reciprocal
    lattice vector.
  - `valence_band_maximum(bands, n_valence)`.
  - `band_minimum_on_segment(structure, k_start, k_end, band, ecut, terms)`
    returns `(t, energy)`, with t ∈ [0, 1] and a 0-based band index.

**Tests that go beyond the theory post's list.** Each tests the theory more
sharply:

- *Supercell folding.* The 8-atom conventional cell at Γ must reproduce the
  primitive spectra at Γ and the three X points exactly. This exercises the
  general 1/Ω per-atom structure factor with 8 atoms, which a hard-coded
  two-atom CB normalisation would fail.
- *1/Ω normalisation alone.* A single atom at the origin must give
  v̂(|G|)/Ω, checked with a test-only Gaussian pseudopotential.
- *Independent NumPy model.* `tests/support/cohen_bergstresser.py` implements
  the model in the paper's own form. The package's Hamiltonian matrix and
  eigenvalues must match it to 1e-13 and 1e-10 Ha. This NumPy model was itself
  checked against Table I before any package code existed.

The mechanical 1a test updates (approved in the API rounds): `Lattice.fcc(a)`
becomes `fcc_lattice(a, unit="Bohr")`, `band_structure(lattice, ...)` becomes
`band_structure(empty(lattice), ...)`, and test-only terms take
`prepare(structure, basis_k)`. No test logic changed.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1b implementation

**The `bind` hook (agreed during implementation).** The coupling vectors of
the matrix-free local potential depend on the cell, and their number fixes an
array shape. Inside `jit` the cell is traced, so they cannot be computed in
`prepare`. The agreed `validate` hook returned nothing, so it could not carry
them. After a question to the project lead, terms gained an optional
`bind(structure) -> term`, which `band_structure` calls on the host before
tracing. `LocalPotential.bind` validates and returns a copy carrying the
coupling vectors as integer leaves. Called outside `jit` (for example through
`hamiltonian(...)` directly), `prepare` binds on the fly. It raises a clear
error if it is reached under tracing without having been bound.

**Which couplings are kept.** `bind` keeps every Miller vector within the
largest support at which some species' form factor is non-zero. It does *not*
drop vectors whose structure factor happens to vanish for the current
positions, such as shell 4 in diamond. Doing so would freeze the current
positions into the operator and silently break derivatives with respect to
positions. For CB Si the result is 44 vectors, independent of the cutoff.

**Neighbour search.** Miller indices are encoded as int64 keys with radius
2¹⁹. That is safely below overflow: (2²⁰+1)³ ≈ 1.2e18 < 9.2e18. Padded entries
get the maximum int64 as their key, so they can never match. A neighbour is
found by `searchsorted` on the sorted keys, which is jittable and vmappable.

**Safe norm.** |G| is computed with a guarded square root, so autodiff
through G = 0 gives a finite gradient rather than NaN. This matters for cell
derivatives later.

**Mutation testing.** Planted bugs that were caught:

- the structure-factor sign
- 1/(2Ω) normalisation
- Rydberg used as Hartree
- Ω_at = Ω
- the guard disabled
- weights ignored

Two survived:

- *Coupling direction m+d instead of m−d.* This builds conj(H), whose
  eigenvalues are identical, so no spectrum test can see it. With the
  symmetric origin, Ṽ is real and the mutant is exactly the correct code. It
  is still a real defect: it is the crystal inverted through the origin, and
  would flip forces later. I added `test_matrix_elements_are_v_of_g_minus_g_prime`,
  an entry-by-entry check of ⟨G|V|G′⟩ = Ṽ(G−G′) for an asymmetric
  structure with complex Ṽ. It kills the mutant. This adds a test; no
  existing test was changed.
- *Padding keys not excluded.* Benign as the code stands: real entries come
  first, the sort is stable, and so a match always lands on the real G = 0
  entry. The explicit exclusion stays as a guard that does not depend on that
  ordering.

**Test correction (raised and agreed).** The property test of
`from_cartesian` unit consistency compared cells with a purely relative
tolerance. Hypothesis found a cell with subnormal entries (1e-310) that the
conversion arithmetic flushes to zero. The agreed fix is an absolute floor of
1e-14·max|A|. The case is pinned as an `@example`.

**Validation document.** The first band plot placed the published Δ₁ marker
relative to the *last* Γ tick. That was my bug: a dict keyed by tick label, and
the path visits Γ twice. The validation document now asserts the tick order
and indexes ticks by position. It also asserts all its interpretive claims
(Table I within tolerance, convergence below 1 meV at 6 Ha, parities), so a
regression breaks the render.

## 2026-11-05: Hypothesis example budgets scale with the profile

**Problem.** Every property test set a literal `max_examples`. A per-test
setting overrides the profile, so `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci` changed nothing: the
profile's own `max_examples` reached no property test at all.

**Decision.** The per-test numbers are kept, because they encode relative cost.
Most of that cost is JAX compiling for each new array shape, and the slowest
test takes about 12 s at 10 examples. They become *base* budgets that
`tests/support/budget.py` multiplies by the active profile's factor:
`@settings(max_examples=examples(10))`.

| Profile | Factor | Use |
|:--|--:|:--|
| `default` | 1 | local runs; the definition of done (property tests about 80 s) |
| `ci` | 5 | before a merge, or on CI hardware |
| `deep` | 20 | occasional exhaustive runs |

Tests without a stated budget get 50 × factor through the profile itself.

**Guards.** An unknown `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE` raises an error at conftest load
instead of silently falling back to the default. A unit test walks the AST of
every test file and fails on a literal `max_examples`, so the override cannot
creep back. A planted literal confirmed that the guard catches it.

**Rejected alternatives.** Dropping the per-test counts would run every test at
the same count, making expensive tests dominate the default run. A pytest
plugin that rewrites settings would be harder to follow, for no gain.

## 2026-11-05: Concepts section and the rule for its code

**Decision.** A new docs section, `docs/concepts/`, holds teaching explainers.
The first is on pseudopotentials, and the second will cover the matrix-free
Hamiltonian. Unlike theory and validation documents, these posts implement the
physics themselves in NumPy/SciPy, with the code shown. The user's reasoning:
code is a second representation of the maths, and the package should stay
clean for its purpose rather than grow functions that only serve teaching.
`CLAUDE.md` records the rule:

- The code in concept posts is not tested and is not a reference.
- jaxdft never depends on it or is shaped by it.
- The posts still assert the claims they make about their own computations.

**Pseudopotential post: two things the computation corrected.**

- **The pseudopotential's repulsive core.** My first draft said the
  pseudopotential becomes repulsive at the centre for large core radii. The
  computed potentials show the opposite. The centre is repulsive only in a
  middle window of r_c, from about 1.1 to 2.1 Bohr. Below that window, near the
  outermost 3s node, it plunges, and above it, it relaxes into a shallow well.
- **Transferability against r_c.** The first draft also assumed that
  transferability worsens monotonically with r_c. The error in the 4s level has
  a minimum near 1.2 Bohr instead.

The text now states both results from the data, and the document asserts them.

**Numerics.** The logarithmic derivative first came from Numerov integration,
while the eigenvalues came from the three-point finite-difference matrix. For
the all-electron atom the two discretisations disagree at the steep core, by
about 0.02 in D at the reference energy. That broke the comparison, although
the pseudo channels agreed. The outward integration now uses the same
three-point recurrence as the eigensolver, so at an eigenvalue it reproduces the
eigenvector exactly. With that change, the Hamann–Schlüter–Chiang identity
holds to about 1e-6.

**Sources checked.**

- The HGH Si LDA parameters (r_loc = 0.44, C1 = −7.33610297) and the local
  form-factor formula: HGH 1998, eq. 5 and Table I, cross-checked against
  CP2K's `GTH_POTENTIALS` entry `Si GTH-PADE-q4`.
- The Si core levels: X-ray Data Booklet, Table 1-1.
- The GTH 1996 Si parameters differ from HGH 1998: four C terms against one.
  The post uses HGH.
- An overlay of the Lindhard-screened HGH local part on the Cohen–Bergstresser
  form factors was dropped as misleading. The empirical local potential absorbs
  the s and p nonlocal repulsion. The post now shows the mismatch as a table
  and explains it.

**Test defect fixed (raised and agreed).** Hypothesis drew a 6-Bohr cell with
k = 0 for `test_matrix_elements_are_v_of_g_minus_g_prime`. At 1 Ha that basis
is only G = 0, so V is real and the test's precondition failed before anything
about the code was tested. The precondition is now `assume(...)`, and that
cell is pinned as an `@example`. The coupling-direction check itself is
unchanged.

## 2026-11-05: Ruff formats the code in documents; annotations replace comments

The visible code in the documents had lines past 100 columns, so code blocks
scrolled sideways. Ruff 0.17 can format Python code blocks inside Markdown as a
preview feature. It handles Quarto's ```` ```{python} ```` fences, leaves `#|`
cell options alone, and accepts `.qmd` through an `extension = {qmd =
"markdown"}` mapping in its config. `docs/ruff.toml` holds that config with an
80-column limit, so the package sources keep their own style and nothing outside
`docs/` is reformatted. Ruff was added as a dev dependency.

Ruff does not wrap comments, docstrings or strings, and when it splits a
statement it moves a trailing comment after the closing parenthesis. Both
needed hand fixes. In the concept post, explanatory comments became Quarto code
annotations (`code-annotations: hover`, set site-wide), which keeps the code
short and puts the explanation in prose. Ruff leaves the `# <n>` markers on
their lines. One validation cell gained a small `parity_sign` helper in place of
a nested conditional inside an f-string.

## 2026-11-05: Pseudopotential post revised after review

Claude Science reviewed the pseudopotential concept post
(`docs/concepts/reviews/review_pseudopotentials.md`). Every number it quoted
reproduced when re-run from the post's code. Changes:

- **Cutoff criterion.** The post measured cost by the norm missing above
  E_cut. Energy convergence weights each q by an extra q²/2 and needs 2–7×
  more for the pseudo-orbitals, and about 20–60× more for the all-electron
  ones. Both criteria are now plotted, and the prose quotes the
  kinetic-energy numbers. The model pseudo-3s at r_c = 1.6 Bohr needs about
  27 Ha, which matches the range real silicon pseudopotentials use.
- **Transform.** The kinetic-energy criterion needs q far beyond the old grid
  (160 Bohr⁻¹), which the all-electron orbitals ran into. All transformed
  orbitals are s orbitals, so the Hankel transform is a sine transform, and
  `scipy.fft.dst(type=1)` gives it exactly for the radial grid function, up to
  π/h. This also removed the grid dependence the review found in the 1s
  number. The all-electron kinetic-energy cutoffs are still near the grid's
  resolution (the bare Coulomb 1s comes out 9% below the analytic value), so
  they are quoted to one figure, and that check is asserted.
- **Non-monotonic cutoff.** With the kinetic-energy criterion, the cutoff
  rises slightly between r_c = 1.3 and 1.4 Bohr. The missing fraction is a
  tail sum, so this is a property of the pseudo-orbitals, not of the
  threshold search. A jump in u‴ at r_c (which Kerker does not match) is a
  plausible cause, but the evidence was mixed, so the post states the bump
  without a mechanism. The monotonic assert became "no step up larger than
  10%".
- **Trade-off chart.** The two charts against r_c became one curve of 4s error
  against cutoff, parameterised by r_c. The dominated region below the best
  r_c is asserted.
- **Real cutoffs.** Added a table of PseudoDojo standard-table hints
  (ONCVPSP-PBE-PDv0.4, `standard.djson`, `hints.{low,normal,high}.ecut`, in Ha
  per the PseudoDojo FAQ). These are quoted citations, not computed results.
- **Text.**
  - Added screening/unscreening and norm conservation's role for the density.
  - Corrected the semilocal matrix element to a single radial integral per
    pair of plane waves.
  - Added the ghost-state caveat [Gonze, Stumpf and Scheffler 1991].
  - Described ultrasoft and PAW separately.
  - Added the other limits of the Lindhard comparison, and the model core
    being deeper than real Si.
  - Added the limits of the frozen core, the potential's kink at r_c, and the
    parameter count of the Kerker form.
  - Removed a stray BEL byte (`\a` from `\approx`, mangled on the way in). A
    scan of all tracked files found no other control characters.
- `ecut_for` now raises when the threshold is never reached, instead of
  returning the first grid point.

## 2026-11-05: Concept post on the matrix-free Hamiltonian

Second concept post, `docs/concepts/matrix_free_hamiltonian.qmd`. Notes on
choices made while writing it:

- **Tied to jaxdft.** The post's NumPy H for Cohen–Bergstresser silicon at Γ
  is asserted equal to `dense_matrix` (rows matched by Miller index), and its
  gather finds the same 44 coupling vectors as `LocalPotential.bind`. Only
  the post depends on jaxdft, never the other way round.
- **Smooth potential.** The contrast to Cohen–Bergstresser is the HGH Si local
  part from the pseudopotential post. It is used only as a typical form
  factor; without screening or a nonlocal part it is not a physical
  Hamiltonian, and the post says so.
- **Zeros are structural.** The draft claimed a smooth potential fills every
  coupling. The assert caught that 25% of couplings at 3 Ha vanish because
  diamond's structure factor cos(G·τ) is zero there. The assert now checks
  that the smooth potential is non-zero exactly where the structure factor
  is.
- **FFT grid.** The FFT product cuts V at |d| ≤ 2G_max and uses 4n + 1 points
  per axis, which reproduces the dense product to rounding error. A 1D toy
  asserts that the cyclic convolution is exact from M = 4K + 1 and wrong at
  4K.
- **LOBPCG.** `scipy.sparse.linalg.lobpcg` wraps the FFT product in a
  `LinearOperator`, with a diagonal 1/(T + 1 Ha) preconditioner
  [Payne et al. 1992]. Two buffer vectors are used, because a block of
  exactly 8 stalled just above tolerance. Iterations are counted until the
  8 wanted residuals converge, not until scipy stops, since the buffer
  vectors otherwise inflate the count. scipy returns residual norms with a
  complex dtype for complex operators; the post takes their absolute value.
- **Timing claims.** Timings depend on the machine. The text quotes fitted
  slopes and the dense–FFT crossover from the measurements. It asserts only
  that the dense slope is the steepest, and chooses its wording for "dense is
  still faster at N = 749" from the measured comparison.

## 2026-11-06: An Ideas section, and a first post on a GP basis

`docs/ideas/` is a new section for exploratory tests of speculative methods.
It follows the concept-post rules (its own NumPy/SciPy code, untested, never
imported by jaxdft, with asserts on its own claims). It adds two rules, now in
`CLAUDE.md`: each post states the limits of its test, and a promising result
reaches the package only through a milestone.

The first post, `ideas/gp_basis.qmd`, treats grid values as GP observations
and uses the posterior mean as a Galerkin basis. It compares this with
sinc-DVR and finite differences on two 1D wells. Numerical choices made while
writing it:

- **Basis in the Gaussian form.** The cardinal functions span the same space
  as Gaussians centred on the nodes, so the post computes in the Gaussian
  basis, where S and T are analytic. Near-dependence is handled by canonical
  orthogonalisation with a relative threshold on the overlap eigenvalues.
- **Potential matrix by fine-grid trapezoid, not Gauss–Hermite.** The first
  version used 80-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature. Its error grows with the
  kernel width, and the nearly singular overlap matrix amplifies it, so wide
  kernels gave energies thousands of Ha *below* the exact values. A
  variational optimiser of the length scale would have selected exactly
  those. The averages depend only on the midpoint of each pair, which lies
  on a half-spacing grid, so only 2N − 1 one-dimensional integrals are
  needed. The trapezoid rule on a fine grid makes them accurate to rounding,
  and an assert checks the matrices against brute-force quadrature. The post
  keeps the Gauss–Hermite run as a cautionary curve.
- **Rounding floor.** "Below exact" is judged against a floor of 1e-10 Ha,
  about ε_mach·|ε|/√rcond for the deepest level, because canonical
  orthogonalisation scales the weakest kept directions by 1/√s. Without it,
  rounding at the 5e-12 level was flagged as a broken bound.

## 2026-11-06: Saddle-point example in the matrix-free post

The LOBPCG section of the matrix-free post now explains why iterative solvers
find the *lowest* eigenvectors, given that the residual vanishes at every
eigenvector. Every eigenvector above the lowest is a saddle of the Rayleigh
quotient, and Ritz values are upper bounds (Courant–Fischer). A 60-point
finite-difference particle in a box shows the failure mode. Started from an
exactly odd vector, single-vector LOBPCG converges by its residual (below
1e-8) to the first excited state. It escapes only when rounding error has
grown an even component. The post asserts that the odd start reaches the
wrong eigenvector with a converged residual, and that a start seeded with
1e-12 of a random vector escapes. Whether the purely odd start escapes within
the run depends on rounding, so the sentence describing it is computed rather
than asserted.

For jaxdft this means a future iterative solver should start from random
vectors with every symmetry present, and keep the dense-versus-iterative
agreement tests at small sizes: a converged residual alone would not catch a
missed state.

## 2026-11-06: Milestone 2a public API, agreed before implementation

Settled in two question rounds with the project lead after the 2a theory
post was reviewed, before any 2a test or code was written. The physics is in
the [2a theory post](../theory/02a_scf_h2.qmd); this entry records the shape of
the code.

**The FFT grid lives on `PlaneWaveBasis`.** `PlaneWaveBasis.build(...,
fft_shape=None)` computes the minimal grid from the no-wraparound rule,
rounded up to 2·3·5-smooth sizes. An explicit `fft_shape` overrides it, for
the undersized-grid positive control and for matching DFTK later. The shape
is static. The basis gains transforms between coefficients and grid values.
`CLAUDE.md` already says the basis owns real/reciprocal transforms. A separate
grid object was rejected, because nothing would tie a grid to its basis.

**Density-dependent terms define only an energy.** The local pseudopotential,
Hartree and XC each implement `energy(structure, basis, ρ)`. The potential is
`(N_tot/Ω) ∂E/∂ρ_j` by `jax.grad` with respect to the grid density. Several
properties then hold by construction instead of by care: the potential is
the exact derivative of the discrete energy, the α term is in the
Hamiltonian, Janak's theorem holds, and direct and double-counting energies
agree at self-consistency. GGA potentials come for free later. The cost is a
reverse-mode FFT pair per evaluation. The `CLAUDE.md` wording on XC was
updated to describe this design. Explicit DFTK-style (energy, potential)
pairs were rejected: the α finding in the review showed how small, and how
hard to see, a G = 0 or Ω mismatch between the two would be. Operator terms
(kinetic now, nonlocal in 2b) keep the 1a/1b `prepare`/`apply` protocol.

**`energy(structure, ...)` runs the SCF inside.** `jax.grad(energy)(structure)`
gives forces, cell gradients and weight gradients. Inside, the converged
orbitals are `stop_gradient`ed and the density is rebuilt from them and the
λ-dependent occupations. A `custom_vjp` for implicit differentiation replaces
the stop later, without changing the entry point. The SCF loop is therefore
traceable (`lax.while_loop`). A host-facing `scf(...)` returns the full
result (density, orbitals, eigenvalues, occupations, energy breakdown,
iteration count, convergence flag) for runs and inspection. The two-step
alternative (run `scf`, then differentiate `total_energy(s, result)`) was
rejected. It silently gives wrong forces if `s` is not the structure the SCF
ran on, and that cannot be checked under tracing.

**Weight-derivative side: `energy(..., side=-1 | +1)`.** The occupation
function has a `custom_jvp` whose slope at integer N_el is one-sided, so plain
`jax.grad` returns the HOMO or the LUMO side, both from the same SCF result. A
hand-coded `weight_derivatives` adding Z·ε± was rejected as a separately
implemented derivative.

**Failure under tracing is NaN.** If the SCF does not converge, the
eigensolver does not converge, or the gap guard trips, `energy` returns NaN
and its gradients are NaN. `scf()` on the host raises a descriptive error for
the same conditions, and it is the diagnostic tool. Rejected: `has_aux`,
whose check every call site could forget, and `checkify`, which is clunky for
a user-facing function.

**GTH pseudopotentials come from a parser and a vendored file.**
`parse_hgh(path) -> GTH` reads the HGH/GTH text format. The hydrogen file
`h-q1.hgh` ships verbatim as package data, copied from JuliaMolSim
PseudoLibrary (`pseudos/hgh_lda_hgh/`), and a test pins its hash. A file with
nonlocal projectors raises `NotImplementedError` until 2b extends the
parser. The protocol gains the ionic charge (`None` for Cohen–Bergstresser,
which has no point ions) and α (0 for Cohen–Bergstresser, its V₀ = 0
convention). A typed-in Python builder was rejected because of the
transcription risk: α is a 0.5 % residue of a cancellation and sensitive to
the last digits.

**Ewald is a term, and there is a model builder.** `lda_terms(pseudos)`
returns `(Kinetic(), AtomicLocal(pseudos), Hartree(), Xc(lda_pw92), Ewald(pseudos))`.
Energies are reported as a dict keyed by term name, mirroring DFTK's
breakdown. Building the energy raises if the terms include an ionic
pseudopotential but no `Ewald`, because that total is not the energy of a
neutral cell.

**Two local-pseudopotential terms.** `LocalPotential` (1b, neighbour gather,
finite support only) stays as an operator term. `AtomicLocal` is the new FFT
energy term and accepts any pseudopotential. The gather-versus-FFT test on
Cohen–Bergstresser bands goes through public APIs. `band_structure` gains an
optional `density` argument, which evaluates the potentials of energy terms
at a fixed density. 2b needs it for silicon bands from a converged density.
A single class switching implementation by support was rejected as hidden
behaviour.

**Decided without a question round, open to change while writing the tests:**

- SCF settings are a frozen dataclass, `SCFOptions(tol, max_iter, n_bands,
  mixer, eigensolver)`, static under `jit`. `mixer` is `Anderson(depth,
  beta)`; simple mixing is `depth=0`. `n_bands` defaults to the occupied count
  plus one.
- The eigensolver keeps the 1a signature, `(apply, dim, n_bands)`, with an
  optional initial block for warm starts. `lobpcg` and `dense_eigensolver`
  both satisfy it. The first SCF step starts LOBPCG from random vectors (see
  the saddle-point entry above). Later steps warm-start.
- Orbitals keep the 1a layout `(n_k, n_pad, n_bands)`, k first. The density is
  `(N1, N2, N3)` and real.
- The molecule builder is `structure/builders/dimer.py`:
  `dimer_in_box(species, bond_length, box, axis=2)`. It puts the bond centre on
  a grid point at the box centre, for the D4h symmetry tests.
- Unit conversions are added to `units.py` for Å (bond lengths, already
  present) and cm⁻¹ with the proton mass (harmonic frequencies), each with a
  round-trip test.

## 2026-11-06: Milestone 2a acceptance tests, written before implementation

The 2a tests were written from the theory post and the agreed API, and they
fail until the implementation exists. All 179 earlier tests still pass. The
tolerances, each with its derivation, are in `tests/support/tolerances.py`.
Shared H₂ setups, with session-cached SCF runs, are in `tests/support/h2.py`.

Writing the tests fixed some details the API rounds had left open:

- **Grid transforms are unnormalised index operations.**
  `basis_k.to_grid(c)` is Σ_G c(G) e^{2πi m·j/N}, with no Ω^{-1/2} and no
  1/N. `from_grid` is its inverse, restricted to the basis and zero on
  padding. The basis stays lattice-free, as in 1a. Ω enters only in
  `electron_density(lattice, basis, orbitals, occupations, kweights)`.
- **A grid below the rule needs `allow_aliasing=True`.** Otherwise `build`
  raises. That keeps the undersized-grid positive control explicit. A grid
  too small to hold the basis itself always raises.
- **`GTH.local(0)` returns α.** The G = 0 entry is then finite, with a finite
  gradient. `CohenBergstresser` gains `ionic_charge = None` and `alpha = 0`.
- **`ewald_energy(structure, charges, eta=None)` is a pure function** beside
  the `Ewald` term, so the Madelung and η tests need no basis.
- **Energy terms** implement `energy(structure, basis, density)`.
  `term_potential(term, structure, basis, density)` returns V(r), real and
  float64. `hamiltonian(...)` and `band_structure(...)` take `density=`, where
  `None` means a zero density. `AtomicLocal` also exposes `coefficients`
  (analytic, any Miller indices) and `grid_coefficients`, which are zero on
  the Nyquist planes.
- **SCF interface.** `SCFOptions(tol, max_iter, n_bands, mixer, eigensolver,
  min_gap)`. `scf(structure, basis, terms, options, density0=None)` returns an
  `SCFResult` carrying `density`, `orbitals`, `eigenvalues`, `occupations`,
  `energies`, `total_energy`, `residual`, `n_iter`, `converged` and
  `eigen_residuals`. `total_energy(structure, basis, terms, orbitals,
  occupations)` returns `(E, breakdown)`. The fixed-point solver is
  `fixed_point(F, x0, mixer, tol, max_iter, project=None)`, and its `project`
  hook carries clip-then-renormalise. `aufbau_occupations(n_el, n_bands,
  side)`.
- **Eigensolvers** take `(apply, dim, n_bands, *, x0=None, preconditioner=None,
  ...)`. The SCF computes eigenpair residuals itself, so solvers keep
  returning `(eigenvalues, vectors)`. LOBPCG's default start is a fixed-seed
  random block, so runs are reproducible.
- **XC.** `jaxdft.xc.lda` holds `LDA`, `lda_x` (exchange only, used for the
  analytic jellium check) and `lda_pw92`. Each returns `(energy density,
  potential)` when called, and the energy per electron from `.eps`. The PW92
  parameters are stored as published, in `PW92_UNPOLARISED`. The libxc
  comparison is deferred (decision 11), so the acceptance check for now is
  an independent transcription of the PW92 formula in the test.
- **Units.** The energy unit `"cm-1"`, plus `HARTREE_IN_INVERSE_CM` and
  `PROTON_MASS_IN_ELECTRON_MASS` (CODATA 2022).
- **Cross-check values.** Two numbers in `test_scf_h2.py` come from the two
  independent NumPy implementations written from the post: the throwaway
  check and the review. They are E = −1.1048807274 Ha (tolerance 1e-7) and the
  HOMO–LUMO gap 0.347192 Ha (tolerance 1e-6). They are labelled as
  cross-checks, not reference values: they test the implementation against
  the same specification, not the physics. The same applies to the H₂-cell
  Ewald energy, 0.126737138563 Ha.
- **The vendored HGH file** is pinned by its SHA-256 hash, with provenance in
  `src/jaxdft/pseudo/data/README.md`.
- **Slow tests.** The egg-box, grid-rule and derivative tests run many SCFs at
  the test size and are marked `slow`. They still run in the default suite.

## 2026-11-06: Milestone 2a implementation

The SCF, energy terms, grid, LOBPCG and differentiable energy are implemented, and
all 330 tests pass (2 min 13 s on the laptop CPU). These are the decisions made
during implementation that the API rounds did not settle.

**Static shapes under `jax.grad`.** In JAX 0.12, values are not concrete inside
`jax.grad`, even without `jit`: `float(x)` raises. So every array size must
come from static data. Two places were affected.

- **Ewald truncation.** Without a traced cell, `ewald_energy` sizes its sums on
  the host. The `Ewald` term takes static ranges from the FFT grid instead: the
  grid's reciprocal box, plus enough real-space images to cover a cell three
  times more skewed than a cube. η is chosen under tracing to balance the two
  truncations. A traced check (η r_R ≥ 6.5 and r_G/2η ≥ 6.5) makes the energy
  NaN if the ranges are insufficient. The failure is loud, consistent with the
  2a convention.
- **Band count in `energy()`.** It is ceil(Σ Z/2) + 1 from the *unweighted*
  charges, so it assumes λ ≤ 1. `scf()` is host-side and uses the actual
  N_el. Finite differences at λ = 1 + δ go through `scf()`, so they are
  unaffected.

**XC vacuum threshold.** Below ρ = 1e-40 the functional is set to zero. At
1e-300 the derivative of r_s ∝ ρ^(-1/3) overflows and the gradient became NaN.
At 1e-40 everything is finite and ρε is about 1e-53. The smallest density in
the H₂ boxes is about 5e-14.

**Warm starts without mixing them.** `fixed_point` accepts an F that carries
auxiliary state, `F(x, aux) -> (f, aux)`. The SCF uses it for the previous
orbitals (LOBPCG warm starts). The state the solver mixes is still only the
density, so implicit differentiation can later wrap the same solve. The first
SCF step starts LOBPCG from a fixed-seed random block, masked to the basis.
Padding components then stay exactly zero, because `apply_H` decouples them.

**LOBPCG.** Rayleigh–Ritz on [X, W, P]. W and P are orthogonalised against X
twice, scaled to unit columns, and orthonormalised by the eigendecomposition
of their Gram matrix. Directions with relative Gram eigenvalue below 1e-12
are dropped and pushed to a large Ritz value, which keeps shapes fixed. X is
re-orthonormalised by QR every iteration. The SCF preconditioner is
r/(max(T_G − ε, 0) + 1), with T from the kinetic diagonal. Eigensolver
tolerance: 0.05 τ_SCF, floored at 2e-14 (rounding at ‖H‖ ~ 20 Ha). The SCF
fails if any final residual exceeds 0.1 τ_SCF, floored at 1e-13.

**Ewald self-exclusion.** The real-space sum originally dropped every pair at
zero distance. A Hypothesis case with three coincident atoms showed that this
silently gave a finite energy for distinct coincident charges, whose physical
energy is infinite. Only i = j at R = 0 is excluded now.

**Two corrections to the acceptance tests.** Both were errors in the tests,
not in the expectations behind them.

- `test_anderson_beats_simple_mixing_on_a_slow_contraction` capped simple
  mixing at 500 iterations. With β = 0.7 the slowest mode contracts by 0.965
  per step, so reaching 1e-10 takes about 715 steps. The cap is now 2000. The
  assertion that Anderson (56 steps) is more than three times faster is
  unchanged.
- The Ewald property tests now `assume` a minimum image separation of
  0.5 Bohr. Coincident point charges lie outside the input domain, because
  their energy is infinite. That corresponds to the fix above.

**Measured margins** (test size, H₂ at d = 1.45 Bohr):

| Quantity | Measured | Review | Tolerance |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Total energy vs. NumPy cross-check | 1e-10 Ha | — | 1e-7 Ha |
| FD force error, symmetric | 1.8e-7 Ha/Bohr | 1.8e-7 | 1e-6 |
| FD force error, distorted (worst component) | 4.3e-7 Ha/Bohr | — | 1e-6 |
| Net force, off-grid placement | 7e-10 Ha/Bohr | 2.5e-11 | 1e-8 |
| Weight derivative, HOMO side | 2.9e-7 Ha | 2.9e-7 | 1e-5 |
| Weight derivative, LUMO side | 4.1e-6 Ha | 4.1e-6 | 1e-5 |
| Egg-box, rule grid (N = 30) | 5e-11 Ha | 2e-11 | < 1e-9 |
| Egg-box, undersized (N = 24) | 3.2e-6 Ha | 8.4e-6 | > 1e-6 |
| Max eigenpair residual | 2e-11 Ha | — | < 1e-10 |

The undersized egg-box is 2.6 times smaller than the review measured, probably
because of where the molecule sits relative to the coarse grid. It still
clears the threshold by a factor of 3. The LUMO-side weight derivative has the
thinnest margin, a factor of 2.4, as the post predicted. The fallback if it
proves fragile remains Richardson extrapolation.

**Timing.** An H₂ SCF at the test size (1503 plane waves, 30³ grid) converges
in 8 Anderson steps. The first call takes about 1.2 s including compilation;
repeat calls take 0.15 s. This goes into `performance.qmd` with the
validation document.

## 2026-11-06: Milestone 2a validation document

**The grid bound separated from its rounding.** `rule_fft_shape` returned
the no-wraparound bound already rounded up to a 2·3·5-smooth size, and
`PlaneWaveBasis.build` checked user grids against that rounded value. A
grid of exactly the bound ($N$ = 29 at the acceptance size) was rejected
unless the caller passed `allow_aliasing=True`, which says the opposite of
what is true. The bound is now `min_fft_shape`. `rule_fft_shape` rounds it,
and the build check uses the bound itself. A unit test pins 29, 30 and the
rejection of 28. The validation document needs this to mark the bound on
its egg-box scan without restating the formula.

**Bond length and frequency from forces.** The document finds $r_e$ by
Newton's method on $\partial E/\partial d$ from `jax.grad(energy)`. The force
constant comes from central differences of that derivative with a step of
$2\times10^{-3}$ Bohr. At 30 Ha it agrees with a second difference of SCF
energies to $10^{-4}$ relative, which the document asserts. The reduced mass is
$m_p/2$, which reproduces the review's frequencies to the wavenumber.

**Render cost.** The document runs about a hundred SCF and force
calculations, up to 100 Ha (120³ grid) and to $L$ = 16 Bohr at 60 Ha. It
takes about four minutes to render on the development laptop, the slowest
page of the site. Every expensive point backs a claim. The top two cutoffs
show convergence, and the second box-correction cutoff sets the uncertainty
of the best estimate. If render time becomes a problem, the first thing to
drop is the 50 Ha point.

## 2026-11-06: Milestone 2a reference data from DFTK and libxc

Decision 11 of the theory post deferred the reference codes until after
implementation. They are now run, with the tolerances the post fixed
beforehand.

**DFTK setup** (`reference/dftk_h2/`). The Julia project there pins DFTK 0.8.2,
Libxc.jl (libxc 7.0.0), JSON and SHA in its `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml`.
The script follows decision 5:

- `model_DFT(...; functionals=LDA(), symmetries=false)`;
- `fft_size=(30, 30, 30)`, Γ only;
- SCF tolerance 1e-11;
- `FixedBands(n_bands_converge=2)`, so the LUMO is converged rather than
  only computed.

Three details came from reading DFTK, each with a specific question:

- `load_psp(path)` in 0.8.2 dispatches on the file extension and knows
  only `.gth`, not `.hgh` (`src/pseudo/load_psp.jl`). The script therefore
  calls the HGH parser `PspHgh` directly on jaxdft's vendored file, and
  records that file's SHA-256 in the output.
- `energy_psp_correction` (`src/terms/psp_correction.jl`) is
  N_el Σⱼ αⱼ / Ω. The test checks the reported value against that closed
  form, so the convention is confirmed by measurement, as the post asked.
- `FixedBands` (`src/scf/nbands_algorithm.jl`) separates the bands that are
  converged from the bands that are only computed.

The output JSON stores the fractional positions used. The tests build their
structures from those, so the distorted geometry cannot drift between the
Julia and Python definitions.

**libxc setup** (`reference/libxc_lda/`). This uses the same pinned project.
`lda_x`, `lda_c_pw` and `lda_c_pw_mod` are evaluated on 131 densities from
1e-10 to 1e3 Bohr⁻³. `lda_c_pw_mod` is a negative control: the test asserts
that it fails the comparison by more than a factor of 1000 at valence
densities. A tolerance loose enough to accept the wrong parameter set would
make the comparison meaningless, and the control guards against that.

**The libxc tolerance was set after seeing the data.** The theory post fixed
the DFTK tolerances but not a pointwise libxc tolerance. It is 1e-10
relative. The worst measured difference is 6e-12, in correlation at
ρ = 1e-10 (r_s ≈ 1300), where libxc and jaxdft round the same closed form
differently. For ρ ≥ 1e-4 the differences are ~1e-15. The `lda_c_pw_mod`
control sits at 3e-7 to 6e-6 for those densities.

**Results.** Everything agrees four or more orders of magnitude inside its
tolerance:

| Quantity | Worst difference | Tolerance |
|:--|:--:|:--:|
| Energy terms | 5e-11 Ha | 1e-7 Ha |
| Total energy | 4e-14 Ha | 1e-7 Ha |
| Eigenvalues (after the α shift) | 4e-11 Ha | 1e-6 Ha |
| Forces | 2e-11 Ha/Bohr | 1e-6 Ha/Bohr |

Without the α shift the eigenvalues differ by 2.596e-6 Ha, exactly the
amount the theory post predicted. No implementation change was needed.

## 2026-11-06: Mixing behind a protocol

`fixed_point` used to contain the Anderson algorithm itself. `Anderson`
was only a container for `depth` and `beta`, so the solver could not take
any other scheme without being edited. CLAUDE.md asks for approximations
and algorithms behind abstractions, so this was a gap, even though 2a needs
only Anderson. Kerker or Broyden mixing for silicon in 2b would have hit it.

**The protocol.** `Mixer` (`jaxdft.scf.mixing`) has two methods:

- `init(x0) -> state`;
- `update(state, x, r) -> (x_next, state)`, called once per evaluated
  iterate with the projected input `x` and its residual `r = F(x) − x`.

The solver keeps evaluation, projection, the norm and the stopping test.
The mixer only proposes the next input. The state is any pytree with fixed
shapes, since it is carried through `lax.while_loop`. The mixer must be
hashable because it is a static `jit` argument. `Anderson` now implements
the protocol and owns its history; `depth = 0` carries no state at all.

**No change in results.** Iterates and iteration counts on the
fixed-point unit problems are bitwise identical before and after, for
depths 0, 3 and 6. The order of operations (record the pair, then mix) is
the same as before, and the full suite passes unchanged.

**Tests.** `tests/support/mixers.py` defines `AdaptiveLinear`, linear
mixing with adaptive damping. It is deliberately unlike Anderson: its state
is a damping factor and the previous residual norm, not a history. It is
used to test three things:

- the solver converges with it;
- the solver hands the mixer every evaluated input, after projection, with
  its residual;
- the H₂ SCF reaches the same ground state with it as with Anderson.

It lives in the tests, not the package, because nothing yet needs a second
mixer.

## 2026-11-06: SCF extension points

A review for choices fixed inside the SCF, after the mixer
(previous entry), found three more that were cheap to open up. The
results are unchanged. For a distorted H₂ at L = 8 Bohr and 6 Ha, the
following are bitwise identical before and after:

- energy, density, eigenvalues and iteration count;
- the forces from `jax.grad(energy)`;
- a dense-eigensolver run.

**Terms are found by role, not by class name.** The SCF used to require a
term whose class was literally named `"Ewald"`. It took the static ionic
charges from an `ionic_term.pseudos` dictionary. Terms now declare two roles
(documented in `jaxdft.hamiltonian.energy_terms`):

- an *ionic* term provides `ionic_charges`, `static_ionic_charges` and
  `is_ionic`;
- an *ion-ion* term sets `ion_ion = True`.

`AtomicLocal` and `Ewald` declare these roles. A truncated-Coulomb ion-ion
term for isolated systems, for example, now needs no SCF change. The test
uses wrapper terms with other names and no `pseudos` field. With them the
SCF energy, density and forces are bitwise equal to those of the standard
terms.

**The preconditioner is an option.**

- **Before:** the SCF picked out `DiagonalTerm` from the kinetic module by
  `isinstance` and built its preconditioner inline.
- **The diagonal moves into the operator:** `Hamiltonian.diagonal()` sums
  the `diagonal` of the prepared terms that expose one. It is deliberately
  not the full diagonal of H, since that would add the mean of the grid
  potential and change the preconditioner.
- **The formula becomes an option:**
  `diagonal_preconditioner(ham)` (`jaxdft.hamiltonian.preconditioners`)
  is the old formula, now the default of `SCFOptions.preconditioner`.
  `None` turns preconditioning off. The H₂ SCF converges to the same ground
  state without it, as a test checks.
- **`tol` joins the eigensolver interface.** The SCF used to look for a
  `tol` parameter with `inspect.signature`. `dense_eigensolver` now accepts
  it and ignores it, as it already did `x0` and `preconditioner`.

**The initial density is an option.** `SCFOptions.initial_density` is a
callable `(structure, basis, charges) -> ρ`. Its default is
`AtomicGaussians(width=0.8)` in `scf/density.py`, the old Gaussians unchanged.
It replaces `SCFOptions.initial_width`. In 2b a superposition of atomic
densities from the pseudopotential can replace it. With this and the
preconditioner moved out, `scf.py` no longer imports grid helpers from the
basis or anything from the kinetic module.

**Left for the milestones that need them** (from the same review):

- **Occupations as an interface:** smearing needs a theory post on the free
  energy and the Fermi level.
- **k-point weights:** they belong to the 2b k-point design. The SCF still
  assumes uniform weights.
- **A basis-independent SCF:** no second basis exists yet.

The energy breakdown is still keyed by class name, so two terms of one
class share an entry. That is a labelling limitation, and it was not
changed.

## 2026-11-10: SCF observability

Before 2b, the SCF was a black box. `scf` ran one jitted `lax.while_loop`
and returned only the converged state. When a run failed, `SCFError` held a
single message. Silicon with k-points will bring convergence problems that
cannot be diagnosed that way. This entry adds a log and a per-iteration
history. The 2a validation post now shows a complete single-point script
(`examples/h2_single_point.py`) and the log it writes.

**Two channels, one source.** Iterations happen inside the jitted loop, so
Python cannot see them as they run. Both channels are fed from the same
per-iteration values:

- **History (always, pure).** `fixed_point` takes an optional
  `record(x, f, aux) -> dict` and writes its values, together with
  `residual` and `projection`, into buffers of length `max_iter + 1` that
  are carried through the loop. Entries past the last iterate are NaN. `scf`
  truncates them and returns them as `SCFResult.history`. They are also
  attached to `SCFError`, so a failed run can still be inspected.
- **Live lines (only when logging is on).** `fixed_point` also takes a
  traced hook, `on_step(i, values)`. The SCF uses it to issue
  `jax.debug.callback(..., ordered=True)`, which writes one log line per
  iteration while the run is in progress. A run that hangs on HPC therefore
  still shows how far it got. `scf` decides at call time with
  `logger.isEnabledFor(INFO)`. `live` is a static argument, so when logging
  is off the callback is never traced.

**What is recorded per iterate ρᵢ:**

- the Kohn–Sham energy of the orbitals of H[ρᵢ] (the direct functional,
  `total_energy`) and its change from the previous iterate;
- ‖F(ρ) − ρ‖, the quantity actually converged;
- `projection`, the norm of the change made by clip-and-renormalise to the
  mixed density. Anderson combinations conserve charge, so this measures
  clipping. It is rounding-level for H₂;
- HOMO, LUMO and gap over all k;
- the worst eigensolver residual and iteration count over k.

The energy costs one direct-functional evaluation per step. `energy()` (the
differentiable path) neither records nor logs, so forces pay nothing.

**Design points.**

- **stdlib `logging`, library conventions.** The package logs to the
  `jaxdft` logger and attaches a `NullHandler`, so it is silent unless the
  application configures logging. `jaxdft.log_to_file` and
  `log_to_stream` are conveniences. Formatting is in pure functions
  (`jaxdft.output.report`) that are tested without running an SCF. Machine
  details are in `jaxdft.output.environment`.
- **`max_iter` is now static.** It sizes the history buffers, so changing
  it recompiles `_scf_core`. A tolerance change still does not.
- **Compile time is reported separately.** `scf` now calls
  `_scf_core.lower(...).compile()` and then the compiled executable. JAX
  caches both steps (a second `lower().compile()` costs microseconds), so
  repeated calls do not recompile. The log can therefore report
  compilation and the SCF itself separately, which matters on GPU.
- **Wall time without host state.** The live line shows wall time since
  the SCF started. The start time is passed into the compiled function as
  an ordinary argument, `t0`, and handed to the callback. The callback is a
  module-level function, so the jit cache key is stable across calls and no
  mutable timing state is needed.
- **The eigensolver reports iterations** through an additive keyword,
  `return_iterations=True`, which appends the count to the result.
  `dense_eigensolver` returns 0. It is a keyword rather than a new return
  signature, so existing callers (band structures, tests) are unchanged. As
  with `tol`, a custom eigensolver used in the SCF must accept it.
- **Provenance in the header.** The header gives the git commit with
  `+dirty` (cached per process: the running code is the code that was
  imported), the jax/jaxlib versions, backend and devices, process
  index/count, and Slurm/XLA environment variables if set. Every term and
  option is printed through `describe`, which never prints a memory
  address. For that, `GTH` gained a `source` field holding the parsed file.
  The field is excluded from equality and hashing, so it never changes a
  jit cache key.
- **Not done:** a machine-readable JSON-lines sidecar. `SCFResult.history`
  already gives structured access. It can be revisited once runs are
  managed on HPC.

**Cost.** The live lines add a few percent to a steady-state H₂ SCF at
the acceptance size (`performance.qmd`, 'Observability'). The first
version cost 45 %. Profiling traced the extra time to two `git`
subprocesses per call, now cached.

## 2026-11-11: Milestone ladder on the front page, project statistics

The front page now tells the project as a ladder of milestones, and a new
page, `engineering/project_stats.qmd`, shows the effort in numbers.

**One source of truth.** `docs/milestones.yml` lists every milestone: id,
title, one-line capability, status, the time it was reached, and its theory
and validation documents. The front page and the milestone markers on the
statistics page both read it. Adding a milestone means adding one entry
there, plus one `featured.publish(...)` call in its validation document.

**Dates are written in the file, not read from git.** The repository has no
tags, and a date resolved from a commit would be missing in a shallow clone.
The `reached` timestamps were copied once from the commits that completed
each milestone.

**Validation documents publish; the front page only reads.** A validation
document calls `jaxdft.plotting.featured.publish(chart, id, caption=...,
headline=...)` with a chart it has already drawn and one headline number it
has already computed. The call writes the chart (as an embeddable fragment,
resized for the front page) and the numbers to `docs/_results/`, which git
ignores. Nothing is hardcoded and the front page runs no calculation. The
helper sits next to the shared plot style in `jaxdft.plotting`, which is
already documentation-only code.

**The front page is assembled after the render.** `docs/_tools/front_page.py`
is a Quarto `post-render` script. It reads `milestones.yml` and `_results/`
and fills two placeholders in the rendered `index.html`: the ladder and the
small statistics strip. Alternatives considered:

- *The `embed` shortcode.* It needs labelled cells, and for a `.qmd` source
  Quarto executes the source document to obtain the output. With freeze off
  that would run the validation calculations a second time. This was not
  measured; the approach was dropped before testing it.
- *A Quarto listing with a custom template.* A listing shows a static image
  per item, and our charts are altair, so this would need a second, static
  copy of each figure.
- *A Python cell in `index.qmd` reading `_results/`.* Quarto does not promise
  to render the validation documents before the front page, so a fresh clone
  could build the front page before its inputs exist.

The script is idempotent. It fails the render when a completed milestone's
validation document was rendered but published no figure, when a linked
document does not exist, or when an entry in `milestones.yml` is malformed.
If only `index.qmd` is rendered in a fresh clone, the ladder shows a note in
place of the missing figures instead of failing.

**Statistics come from git at render time.** The statistics page walks
`git log` and counts lines per commit with `git grep` on the commit, so no
checkout is needed. The time axis is days since the first commit. In a shallow clone, or
outside a repository, it shows a notice instead of partial numbers, and the
front-page strip falls back to a plain link. Test coverage is not shown: its
history cannot be read from git without re-running the suite at every commit.

**Dependency.** `pyyaml` was added to the `docs` group. It was already
installed as a dependency of Jupyter, but is now imported directly.

**Not done.** There is no CI configuration in the repository, so the
fresh-clone and shallow-clone behaviour was checked by hand only. The reviews
of the theory posts are Markdown files that are not rendered into the site,
so the ladder links to theory and validation but not to the review.

## 2026-11-11: Conversation excerpts on the site

A new section, `docs/conversations/`, shows five excerpts of the Claude Code
sessions in which the project has been developed. One goal of the project is
to show what agentic development of a scientific code looks like, and the
finished documents do not show the exchanges that produced them.

**The data files are the record.** Claude Code keeps session logs under
`~/.claude/projects/`, on one machine, and deletes them after
`cleanupPeriodDays` (30 by default; now raised in the user settings). An
excerpt is therefore extracted once, by `docs/_tools/conversations.py extract`,
into `docs/conversations/data/<name>.json`, which is tracked by git. Which
lines of which session make up an excerpt is listed in
`docs/conversations/excerpts.yml`. Once a log is gone its excerpts can no
longer be re-extracted, so the extractor does not replace an existing data
file unless asked to.

**What an excerpt holds.** The messages of both sides, verbatim; one line per
tool call (its description, or the file it touched); the question rounds with
the options and the answers; and a marker where the session's context was
summarised. It leaves out tool output, the model's reasoning, subagent
transcripts and harness messages. Paths on the development machine are
shortened by a fixed list of patterns. A user message that was an accepted
suggestion rather than typed text is marked as such.

**Rendering is a post-render script**, the same mechanism as the front page.
Each page holds a placeholder that `conversations.py` fills in the rendered
HTML. Alternatives considered:

- *Passing the messages through pandoc.* Claude's replies are written for a
  terminal that renders GitHub-flavoured Markdown. Pandoc's Markdown reads
  `~`, `^`, `@name` and `<word>` differently, so replies would be altered.
  The script uses `markdown-it-py` with HTML disabled instead.
- *A Python cell in each page calling a renderer in the package.* It would put
  a transcript renderer in `jaxdft`, which has nothing to do with it.

Within a reply, headings are rendered as bold paragraphs so they stay out of
the page outline. TeX in a reply is passed to MathJax; because pandoc sees no
math on such a page, the page loads MathJax itself in its front matter.

**Display.** Claude's tool calls and the short notes between them are folded
into one block per turn, with the time it took. What Claude wrote after its
last tool call of a turn is shown in full.

**Dependencies.** `markdown-it-py` and `mdit-py-plugins` were added to the
`docs` group.

**Not done.** The selection is made by hand. The excerpts so far all come
from the first two sessions.

## 2026-11-11: Milestone 2b public API, agreed before implementation

Settled after the [2b theory post](../theory/02b_scf_silicon.qmd) was
reviewed and revised, before any 2b test or code was written. Two choices
went to the project lead; the rest were proposed in the same round and not
objected to. The physics is in the theory post; this entry records the shape
of the code.

**k-point weights live on the basis.** `PlaneWaveBasis.build(...,
kweights=None)` stores a `kweights` leaf of shape `(n_k,)` next to
`kpoints`; `None` means uniform. Weights must be non-negative and sum to 1,
or `build` raises. The weights can then never be paired with the wrong
k-points, `scf` and `energy` keep their signatures, and the weights shard with
the k axis. `total_energy(structure, basis, terms, orbitals, occupations)`
loses its `kweights` argument (no caller passed it).
`electron_density(..., kweights=None)` keeps its optional override, which
defaults to `basis.kweights`. Rejected: weights as an SCF argument (every call
site must pair them with the right basis, uncheckable under tracing), and a
`KGrid` type (room for symmetry data before anything needs it). A band-path
basis carries uniform weights that mean nothing; that is the accepted cost.

**k-grids.** `monkhorst_pack(shape, shift=(0, 0, 0)) -> (kpoints, weights)`
in `structure/kpoints.py`: k = (n + s)/N in fractional coordinates, in
[0, 1), uniform weights. The shift exists for the positive control of the
symmetry argument (theory post); production runs use the Γ-centred grid.

**Nonlocal radial data: a tuple of channels.** A pseudopotential exposes
`channels`, one object per angular momentum. For HGH this is
`HGHChannel(l, r, h)` in `pseudo/gth.py`, with `h` the symmetric coupling
matrix (Ha, a tuple of tuples) and `projectors(q2)` returning the reduced
projectors p̂ᵢ(q)/qˡ, shape `(n_i, *q2.shape)`, Bohr^(3/2+l), as traceable
functions of q² (theory post, decision 7). A pseudopotential without the
attribute, or with `channels == ()`, has no projectors: hydrogen and
Cohen–Bergstresser are unchanged. `GTH(zion, rloc, c, channels=(), source)`
gains the field; `parse_hgh` reads the projector blocks (upper triangles of
h, symmetrised), refuses l > 2 and (l, i) outside the theory post's table
with `NotImplementedError`, and refuses trailing lines it does not understand
with `ValueError`. Rejected: flat per-l methods on the pseudopotential (three
members that must agree), and a pseudopotential that builds whole projector
blocks from Cartesian q (every family would reimplement the solid harmonics
and the q = 0 handling).

**The nonlocal term.** `AtomicNonlocal(pseudos)` in
`hamiltonian/atomic_nonlocal.py`, an operator term (`prepare`/`apply`, the
`B D Bᵀ` product of the theory post). It owns the solid harmonics, the
structure-factor phases and Ω^(-1/2). `lda_terms(pseudos)` includes it only
