when some pseudopotential has channels, so the H₂ breakdown keeps its five
entries. Its energy is reported as `"AtomicNonlocal"`.

**The HGH silicon file** `hgh_lda/si-q4.hgh` is vendored verbatim from
PseudoLibrary, SHA-256 pinned as for hydrogen; `hgh_lda("Si")` loads it.

**Occupations over the grid.** `grid_occupations(eigenvalues, kweights,
n_electrons, *, side=-1, tol=1e-6)` in `scf/occupations.py` replaces the
per-k `aufbau_occupations` inside the SCF and `energy` (the latter stays, for
its own tests). Its definition, which the theory post leaves to the
implementation:

- The reference count N_ref is the even integer nearest to N (halves round
  up). Bands n < N_ref/2 are doubly occupied at every k; that is the band
  filling the gap guard certifies.
- The remainder δ = N − N_ref is removed from the highest occupied states
  (δ < 0) or added to the lowest empty ones (δ > 0), over all k-points, level
  by level. A level is the set of states within `tol` of each other; every
  state of a level receives the same change of f, so Σ w_k Δf_nk = δ. A level
  that fills or empties passes the rest to the next.
- The derivative with respect to N is one-sided at a kink: `side=-1` is the
  level that loses charge as N decreases, `side=+1` the level that gains as N
  increases.

For one k-point with weight 1 this equals `aufbau_occupations`, so every 2a
result is unchanged.

**The gap guard** compares the lowest state of band N_ref/2 with the highest
of band N_ref/2 − 1 over all k-points, at convergence only. The per-iteration
`gap` in the SCF history already is this quantity. `SCFOptions` gains
`degeneracy_tol = 1e-6` (Ha, passed to `grid_occupations`).

**Buffer bands.** `SCFOptions.buffer_bands = 1`. `n_bands` keeps its meaning,
the bands that must converge (default occupied + 1). The eigensolver
iterates `n_bands + buffer_bands` vectors; residuals are checked, and results
returned, for the first `n_bands` only.

**FFT grids compatible with fractional translations.**
`PlaneWaveBasis.build(..., fft_multiple=1)`, an int or a 3-tuple: each N_i is
the smallest 2·3·5-smooth multiple of `fft_multiple[i]` at or above the
no-wraparound bound. Diamond needs 2. Passing it together with an explicit
`fft_shape` raises. The package does not detect symmetry; the caller states
the multiple.

**Supercells.** `supercell(structure, repeats)` in
`structure/builders/supercell.py`: lattice rows aᵢ·nᵢ, the images of the cell
translation by translation (translations outer, atoms inner), species and
weights tiled.

**`band_minimum_on_segment` gains `density=None`**, passed through to
`band_structure`, for the Δ minimum of the self-consistent bands.

**Tests.** Cross-check numbers that both the throwaway check and the review
produced are labelled cross-checks, as in 2a; the test-size energy and grid
gap come from the review alone and say so. The finite-difference tolerances
for the fractional-charge weight derivatives are derived, not measured,
because nobody has run fractional-charge silicon. If one fails during
implementation it is raised with the project lead, not loosened.

## 2026-11-11: Milestone 2b implementation

The nonlocal term, k-point weights on the basis, grid occupations, buffer bands,
`fft_multiple`, `monkhorst_pack` and `supercell` are implemented as agreed in the
API entry above. These are the decisions made during implementation, and the
changes to acceptance tests, each agreed with the project lead.

**The nonlocal operator.** `AtomicNonlocal.prepare` builds B, of shape
`(n_pad, N_proj)`, once per k-point. Its columns are
Ω^(-1/2) e^(-2πi m·f_a) S_lm(q) p̂ᵢ(q)/qˡ, masked to the basis. D is the block
diagonal of λ_a hˡ, repeated for each m. `apply` is B(D(B†ψ)), with no FFT.
The real solid harmonics up to l = 2 are written out as polynomials in
(q_x, q_y, q_z), and the projectors are functions of q², so no |q| and no q̂
appear anywhere. First and second derivatives with respect to the cell,
positions and k at Γ are finite (a property test).

**Grid occupations.** `grid_occupations` is a `custom_jvp`. The value sorts all
candidate states (empty ones for added charge, occupied ones by −ε for removed
charge), groups them into levels where consecutive sorted energies differ by
more than `tol`, and fills levels by a clipped cumulative capacity. Every step is
a traced array operation, so it runs inside the jitted SCF and under `vmap`.
The JVP picks the active level from the side argument, half-open toward the
side, so the derivative at an integer count is exactly one-sided. Eigenvalues
and weights are stop-gradiented. In `energy()` they already are, and the
Hellmann–Feynman argument needs nothing through them.

**SCF changes.** The occupations are recomputed from the eigenvalues at every
iteration, so a fractional frontier follows the current spectrum. The gap guard
uses `frontier_gap`: CBM − VBM over all k-points of the band filling at N_ref,
evaluated at convergence. The history's `homo`, `lumo` and `gap` are the same
quantity at each iteration. The eigensolver iterates `n_bands + buffer_bands`
vectors, capped by the smallest basis. Only the first `n_bands` are checked,
recorded and returned. The SCF error message now quotes the gap over the grid.

**Four acceptance-test changes, agreed with the project lead.** None loosens a
tolerance. Each comes from the new gap guard meeting a state that the theory
post had measured with the 2a per-k guard.

- **The displaced geometry runs on the 3³ grid, not 2³.** On 2³ the
  0.11 Bohr displacement splits Γ₂₅′ and lowers an X-point conduction state
  until the gap over the grid is 0.12 mHa, below `min_gap` = 1 mHa. Per-k gaps
  stay at 72 mHa. On 3³ the gap is 10.3 mHa, the review's value. The post's
  finite-difference force measurements were already made on 3³. On 3³ the
  conduction-side frontier is the time-reversal pair (k, −k), and the test
  asserts that pair instead of a single state.
- **The XC-off net-force control runs with the guard disabled.** Silicon
  without XC is a semimetal on every grid tried: −0.042 Ha (2³) and −0.025 Ha
  (3³) at the ideal geometry. The identity it tests, a vanishing net force when
  only translation-covariant terms remain, holds at any self-consistent fixed
  point with fixed occupations.
- **The XC-off supercell comparison runs with `min_gap` = 1e-4.** Its gap over
  the 2×1×1 grid is +0.33 mHa: positive, so the band filling is the ground
  state.
- **The gap-guard positive control no longer requires convergence.**
  Local-only silicon is rejected for a gap over the grid of −0.063 Ha (the
  review's value). With fixed occupations it also never converges, since a band
  crossing at the Fermi level (smallest per-k gap 10⁻⁴ Ha) makes them slosh.
  Residuals stay at 10⁻³–10⁻¹ after 300 iterations with any mixer tried. The
  theory post's "accepted a converged state" described the 2a SCF stopping at a
  looser tolerance.

Two further corrections were errors in the tests themselves, not in their
expectations: a read-only NumPy view written to, and a count of partially
occupied states that included the empty conduction bands.

**The unmeasured tolerances held.** Both one-sided weight derivatives at the
displaced geometry, and the degenerate valence side at the ideal geometry,
agree with the second-order finite differences within 10⁻⁵ Ha (5×10⁻⁵ for the
degenerate case). The Z × gap identity holds to 10⁻⁸.

## 2026-11-11: Milestone 2b validation document, and an open performance item

**The validation document is sized to its render cost.** Reproducing all of
the theory post's settings at every render would take 20–30 minutes on the
laptop. The 4³ grid at 40 Ha takes 207 s, 6³ at 15 Ha 152 s, and 8³ 423 s.
With the project lead it was decided to keep the document lean and to profile
later. The document renders in about 7 minutes. Its cheaper settings:

- the cutoff scan runs on the 2³ grid; its convergence profile matches the
  post's 4³ table within 10 %;
- the k-scan stops at 4³ and adds the half-shifted 2³ and 3³ grids;
- E(a) uses half-shifted grids, whose density asymmetry does not matter for
  energies.

The post's 20 Ha, 40 Ha and 6³ numbers are quoted, not recomputed. The band
path, 150 k-points with about 760 plane waves each, uses LOBPCG rather than
dense diagonalisation, to keep the render short.

**Units.** `units.py` gains the atomic unit of pressure, E_h/a₀³ in GPa,
from the CODATA 2022 E_h and a₀, for bulk moduli. It is tested against its
derivation and against the CODATA 2018 value, which differs by 2×10⁻⁹
relative because a₀ changed between the two adjustments.

**Open item: superlinear cost in the number of k-points.** At 15 Ha, 6³ takes
6.7 times as long as 4³ for 3.4 times as many k-points and the same number of
SCF steps. The suspected cause, not yet profiled, is memory. The density and
the local-potential application are `vmap`ped over all k-points at once. They
therefore materialise (n_k, N³, n_bands) complex arrays, about 0.3 GB at 6³,
plus FFT workspace. If profiling confirms it, the fix is to accumulate the
density over k-points in chunks (`lax.map` over batches, or a scan), which
keeps k-points a batch dimension for sharding. The performance page now
tracks the cost per k-point and SCF step, so the fix will be measurable. The
validation document can grow back towards the post's settings afterwards.

## 2026-11-12: Towards the next milestone: smearing, metals, graphene (open)

A discussion with the project lead after the 2b validation, recorded as the
beginnings of the next milestone's description. Nothing here is decided. Other
work comes first, and later entries will record what changes.

**What graphene would need today.** Nothing in the SCF, the operators or the
nonlocal part is specific to silicon. `Lattice` takes any vectors, Ewald, the
FFT grid rule and the basis are general, `monkhorst_pack((n, n, 1))` gives a
2D grid, `kpath` takes any labelled points, and carbon's HGH channels (s, p)
are within `HGHChannel`. The missing pieces are small: the vendored
`c-q4.hgh` with provenance, a hexagonal lattice or graphene builder, and
hexagonal special points. Three things are not small:

- *The gap guard.* π and π* touch at K, at the Fermi level. Grids with n a
  multiple of 3 contain K, the grid gap is zero and the guard rejects the run,
  although `grid_occupations` shares the degenerate level correctly. Grids
  without K pass, and fixed occupations are then exact for undoped graphene,
  but convergence in n is slow near the cone.
- *Cost.* Carbon HGH needs a much higher cutoff than silicon, the vacuum
  multiplies the plane-wave count, and a 2D grid without symmetry reduction
  has many k-points. The open k-point scaling item above would bite first.
- *Symmetry.* The 2b analysis of which FFT grid sizes keep the diamond space
  group would have to be redone for the hexagonal group before vanishing
  forces at the ideal geometry can serve as a test.

**Doping by extra electrons.** Today the electron count is always the sum of
the ionic charges (`scf.py`, `n_el` from `ionic_charges`); the per-atom
weights cannot stand in, since they are capped at 1 and scale the
pseudopotential. An `extra_electrons` option would be a few lines. The
electrostatics already follow the standard compensating-background
convention: Hartree and Ewald drop G = 0 with a uniform background, and the
α term of the local part uses the electron count. In bulk this is the usual
model of doping. In a slab the background fills the vacuum too, a known
artefact; quantitative work would need a counter-charge plane or 2D Coulomb
truncation. The occupations are the real obstacle. The extra charge goes
level by level into the lowest conduction levels on the grid, a correct
zero-temperature filling, but without smearing it converges poorly with the
k-grid and level reordering between iterations can stop the SCF converging.
The gap guard, measured at the reference count, would reject every such run.

**The gap guard compared with smearing.** Codes that smear by default, or
leave smearing to the user, have no such guard: occupations follow a Fermi
level, so band overlap across k-points is absorbed rather than silently
wrong, and in an insulator with a gap much larger than the width the cost is
negligible. The guard exists here because smearing does not exist yet, and
because CLAUDE.md asks for one-sided weight derivatives in gapped systems,
which fixed occupations give directly and smearing blends into one value. The
expected split once smearing exists: smearing is the normal path (metals,
doped cells, unknown systems), minimising a free energy that is
differentiable everywhere; fixed occupations remain an option for insulators,
carrying the guard, the one-sided weight derivatives and the Z × gap
identity.

**Candidate next milestone: smearing, validated on aluminium.** Graphene is a
poor first test of smearing: its Fermi surface is two points and its density
of states vanishes at the Fermi level. Aluminium is preferred:

- one atom in the fcc cell, so the existing builders, special points and
  k-paths apply; the HGH Al pseudopotential (3 valence electrons, s and p
  channels) is soft and there is no vacuum;
- a large Fermi surface, which exercises what smearing changes and gives the
  classic k-grid against smearing-width convergence study;
- references on every rung: nearly free-electron bands (linking back to
  milestone 1a), published LDA lattice constant and bulk modulus, and DFTK,
  whose own examples use smeared aluminium;
- silicon as a control: with smearing it must reproduce the fixed-occupation
  result as the width goes to zero.

Questions the theory post would have to settle: the Fermi-level solve and
its derivative (implicit differentiation or a custom JVP); the entropy term,
the variational free energy that `jax.grad` differentiates, and zero-width
extrapolation of energies; the smearing function (Fermi–Dirac, Gaussian,
Methfessel–Paxton, Marzari–Vanderbilt), each trading convergence in the width
against occupations staying in [0, 2]; charge sloshing in metals and whether
a Kerker-type preconditioner is needed (mild in a one-atom cell, likely in
supercells); and how the gap guard and the weight derivatives change when
smearing is on.

**Graphene later.** It fits a later milestone on 2D systems (hexagonal cells,
vacuum, possibly Coulomb truncation), after the k-point performance fix, with
doped graphene as an application of smearing.

## 2026-11-12: Milestone 2b DFTK comparison

**Reference data.** `reference/dftk_si/` follows `reference/dftk_h2/`: a
Julia script, the same pinned environment (DFTK 0.8.2), a README with the
conventions, and a JSON that identifies the pseudopotential by hash. It runs
the two cases of the theory post: the ideal geometry on the 2³ test grid and
the displaced force-test geometry on 3³, the grid the acceptance tests moved
to on 2026-11-11. The post's specification says "the same k-grid", which for
the displaced case is now 3³.

**DFTK API notes (0.8.2).** The k-grid shift is not a keyword of
`PlaneWaveBasis`; it is given through `kgrid=MonkhorstPack(n; kshift=...)`.
With `symmetries=false` DFTK lists every grid point with weight 1/n_k, so
time reversal is not used either; `length(basis.symmetries)` is 1 and is
stored in the JSON. With an explicit `fft_size` the grid is used as given,
which the script asserts, so the review's question about
`symmetries_respect_rgrid` is settled for this comparison.

**k-point labels.** The tests build jaxdft's own `monkhorst_pack` grid in
[0, 1) and match DFTK's [−½, ½) points modulo 1, rather than feeding DFTK's
coordinates to jaxdft. That way the comparison also covers the relabelling
invariance the theory post names as a test, and the plane-wave counts per
k-point are compared after matching.

**Result.** All energy terms, the total, the eigenvalues of the five
converged bands at every k-point and the forces agree to about 10⁻¹¹ in
atomic units, against tolerances of 10⁻⁷ Ha, 10⁻⁶ Ha and 10⁻⁶ Ha/Bohr. The
validation document computes and shows the differences.

## 2026-11-12: Running on a Slurm cluster with shephex; the k-point cost is the eigensolver

**Setup.** Calculations are submitted from the laptop to the biocloud
cluster with shephex's `RemoteSlurmExecutor`. shephex is in its own
dependency group, `cluster`, which is a default group so `uv run hex ...`
works locally. On the cluster a clone of the repository is synced with
`uv sync --no-default-groups --group cluster`, which installs jaxdft
(editable, so a `git pull` updates it), JAX and shephex but not the test or
docs tools. The lock file pins the same shephex version on both sides, which
shephex requires. The Slurm profile (`biocloud-jaxdft-cpu`: 8 CPUs, 16 GB,
the clone's venv, `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu`) lives in `~/.shephex`, not in the
repository, because it holds cluster paths.

**Layout.** `shephex/scripts/<cluster>/` holds the submit scripts (tracked),
`shephex/data/<cluster>/` the experiment directories pulled back (ignored).
shephex 0.5.0 maps the working directory at submission to the profile's
remote directory and recreates the experiments' relative path under it. The
scripts therefore change into their data directory before submitting, so
runs land directly under the remote directory. A local-root option in
shephex would remove that step.

**Two shephex details.** `@shephex.chain` checks for duplicate experiments,
and doing so writes the experiment directories even in a dry run;
`@shephex.hexperiment` does not, so a dry run leaves no files. The scripts
use `hexperiment` for now. `hex report` without `-p` is a live view that does
not exit, so it does not belong at the end of an automated wait.

**Results go through `reference/`.** Cluster results are not reproducible at
render time, so `reference/biocloud_si_kgrid/extract.py` collects them from
the pulled experiments into a tracked JSON, which the performance page reads.
The README there lists the fields and the limits of the measurement.

**The open item of 2026-11-11.** The k-grid scan on biocloud (performance
page, "Milestone 2b on biocloud") reproduces the superlinear cost, and
explains most of it without memory. The k-points are one `vmap` batch, so
the batched LOBPCG runs until the slowest k-point has converged; the summed
eigensolver iterations grow about as fast as the cost per k-point and SCF
step, while the cost per k-point and eigensolver iteration stays flat and
peak memory grows linearly. Chunking the density accumulation would not have
helped. Two standard remedies, neither implemented:

- **An adaptive eigensolver tolerance.** `scf` asks every step for residuals
  of `EIGEN_TOL_FRACTION` × `tol`, 5 × 10⁻¹¹ by default, even while the
  density error is of order one. Tying it to the current density residual
  should cut the iterations of the early steps, where the large grids spend
  most of them.
- **More buffer bands.** `SCFOptions.buffer_bands` is 1. A wider gap between
  the highest converged band and the block edge speeds up the slowest
  k-points.

Either changes the SCF algorithm, so it goes through the milestone workflow.

## 2026-11-12: First GPU runs (V100); LOBPCG's Rayleigh–Ritz step sets a residual floor on GPU

**Setup on aicloud.** The package gains an optional extra `cuda`
(`jax[cuda12]`, Linux only: the CUDA plugin has no macOS wheels, and without
the marker `uv add` tried to install it on the laptop). CUDA 12 rather than
13 because CUDA 13 no longer supports Volta, i.e. the V100. The driver on the
V100 nodes is 580 (CUDA 13.0), which runs the CUDA 12 wheels. The aicloud
clone is synced with every default group plus `cuda`, so the test suite can
run there. The shephex profile `aicloud-jaxdft-v100` (one V100, 8 cores)
sets `JAX_PLATFORMS=cuda,cpu`: with `cuda` alone the SCF fails at its first
log line, because `jax.debug.callback` needs a CPU device to hand values to
Python. A job that starts a second JAX process on the same GPU (pytest from
a shephex job) turns preallocation off, since each process would otherwise
reserve 75 % of the GPU memory.

**Reference data moved.** The k-grid timings now live in
`reference/si_kgrid_scaling/`, one JSON per cluster (`biocloud.json`,
`aicloud.json`) from one `extract.py <cluster>`. The entry above names the
earlier path, `reference/biocloud_si_kgrid/`.

**k-grid scan on the V100** (performance page). Energies agree with the
biocloud CPU runs to rounding at every grid. From 64 k-points up one V100 is
about 12–15 times faster than eight cores, and the cost per k-point and
eigensolver iteration is flat; the lockstep growth of eigensolver iterations
is the same as on the CPU. The eigensolver remains the thing to fix for
large grids, on either device.

**Test suite on the V100** (`reference/aicloud_pytest/`): 634 passed, 3
failed, 5 errors, against 642 passed on the laptop.

- Seven are one problem: every test that runs the SCF at `SCF_TOL_TIGHT` =
  1e-12 needs eigensolver residuals below 1e-13, and LOBPCG on the GPU
  stalls near 1.5e-12 and runs into its iteration cap.
- One is memory: `band_minimum_on_segment` (used by
  `test_conduction_minimum_is_interior_to_gamma_x`) diagonalises 41 k-points
  at once with the dense solver and asks for more than 9.4 GiB in one
  allocation. The same pattern as the k-point batches: everything is
  materialised at once. Open.

**Diagnosis of the residual floor** (`reference/gpu_lobpcg_floor/`). FFTs
and `apply_H` agree between GPU and CPU to rounding, and GPU `eigh` is
accurate to ~1e-15 relative, so the operator is not the cause, and the floor
is real: the CPU measures the same residual for the GPU's orbitals. In a
diagnostic copy of `lobpcg`, moving only the Rayleigh–Ritz `eigh` to the CPU
removes the floor (H₂ and Si converge to ~4e-14 in as many iterations as on
the CPU); moving the Gram `eigh` or the QR and inverse does not. Keeping
everything on the GPU and lowering the penalty on dropped directions from
1e3 to 2 times max|T| also removes it. The mechanism: the penalty makes
‖T‖ about a thousand times larger than the Ritz values we want, and an
`eigh` that is accurate relative to ‖T‖ then has a thousandfold larger
absolute error in the lowest eigenpairs. CPU LAPACK is accurate enough for
this not to show; the GPU solver is not.

`EIGEN_FLOOR` (2e-14, "‖H‖ ε") is a property of the operator; this shows the
attainable residual also depends on the solver's dense steps and the
hardware. Two candidate fixes, neither implemented: a penalty bounded by
the spectrum of T rather than 1e3 max|T| (it must still keep dropped
directions above the wanted Ritz values), or removing dropped directions
from the Rayleigh–Ritz problem. Either changes the eigensolver, and goes
through the milestone workflow together with the k-point work. The
acceptance tests are unchanged.
